nodes.title: Revisions
nodes.body:
January 15, 1990.  T. Czapla; NOAA SEA Division
FLELMR CODE: 1734

SCIENTIFIC NAME: Pogonias cromis
COMMON NAME:  Black drum
OTHER COMMON NAMES:  Sea drum (834); drum (312 581 664); drum fish (664); gray drum, oyster cracker, striped drum, puppy drum, and butterfly drum (692).

nodes.title: CLASSIFICATION
nodes.body:
Phylum:	Chordata
	Class:		Osteichthyes
	Order:		Perciformes
	Family:	Sciaenidae

nodes.title: VALUE
nodes.body:
Commercial:  Historically fished in the Chesapeake Bay area, the species ranked 20th in quantity and 27th in value in 1920 (312).  Presently, important to commercial fishermen in Virginia only as an incidental catch (591).  Also eaten locally in North Carolina but not shipped elsewhere due to its low market value (834).  The majority of the present day catch is in the Gulf of Mexico; the Gulf accounted for 84% of total U.S. landings of black drum from 1950 to 1976 (692).  In Florida, statewide landings of black drum totaled 243,896 pounds worth $102,478 (average price of $0.42 per pound) in 1988 (902).  Approximately 60% of the total catch was landed at ports on the west coast of Florida (902).  Total catch in the Gulf and Caribbean in 1975 was 1,942 tons with Mexico accounting for 1,777 tons and the U.S. totaling 165 tons (791).  Marketed mostly fresh but not highly esteemed as a food fish in the U.S. (791).  The flesh is said to be coarse and not well flavored (312) thus having little commercial value (834 692).  This being true particularly for larger fish, causes the smaller ones to be of more value (692).  Restrictions or bans on the commercial catch of red drum in the Gulf coast states have resulted in greater fishing effort to take this species.

Recreational:  Considered an important game fish by surfcasters, pier and bridge fishermen (788).  Sport catch is much greater than the commercial landings for this species (591 692).  The total estimated recreational catch of black drum for 1986 for the Gulf of Mexico and south Atlantic regions was 1,867,000 fish, and of that total, 1,430,000 fish were caught in the Gulf of Mexico accounting for 77% of the combined catch of Atlantic and Gulf regions (1064).  Florida and Louisiana landings totaled 17% and 81%, respectively, of the Gulf coast recreational landings of black drum (1064).  Daily bag limit is 5 and the length is not less than 14 inches or greater than 24 inches (TL).

nodes.title: Indicator
nodes.body: Ecological Role:  Known to destroy large numbers of oysters on seed reefs and oyster grow-out leases in Louisiana and Mississippi (47 189), and to do great damage to oyster beds in the Chesapeake Bay area (312).  Schools of drums may destroy nearly every oyster on planted grounds in a single night (834).

nodes.title: RANGE
nodes.body:
Overall:  In the Atlantic, from Massachusetts to south Florida, and throughout coastal waters of the eastern and northern Gulf of Mexico (51 312 327 653 788 791 891).  One specimen has been reported from as far north as the Bay of Fundy, Nova Scotia (1065).  Common from Chesapeake Bay to Florida (327 692), with concentrations off the Texas coast (653).  Also found in Cuba, most of the other Antilles (uncommon), and the Atlantic coast of S. America from Guyana to Brazil or Argentina (312 788 791).

Within Study Area:  Black drum are common through the Gulf of Mexico, and commonly inhabit estuarine and nearshore waters throughout Florida (664).  One of the ten most abundant fish species collected in the littoral zone of the upper reaches of Tampa Bay (853).

nodes.title: Movements/Migrations
nodes.body: Black drum are predominantly estuarine inhabitants, and little inter-bay movement has been recorded in Texas waters (653).  Richards (591) considered the species to be migratory along the mid-Atlantic coast, exhibiting a northerly and inshore movement in the spring, and a movement to the south and offshore in late fall.  A similar but less well defined migration may occur in the Laguna Madre area of Texas (653).  Adults display spawning migrations toward Gulf passes in Texas (653), and toward the mouth of the bay in the Chesapeake area (591).  Following spawning, adults disperse back into the estuarine environment at both locations (591 653).  Adverse conditions such as high temperatures, hypersalinity or insufficient food may trigger localized migrations to areas with more favorable conditions (653).

nodes.title: LIFE MODE
nodes.body:
Eggs: are pelagic (368).
Larvae: are also pelagic, and are transported by currents through tidal passes to estuarine waters (9 368).
Juveniles: prefer shallow, turbid, nutrient rich waters (543), and are commonly found in estuaries (791).
Adults: are pelagic throughout the estuaries and bays of the Gulf (139 653), and are often abundant along beaches (791).  At maturity, adults are in constant movement searching for food, which often results in the formation of large schools (591).

nodes.title: Type
nodes.body:
Eggs: are found in both marine and estuarine environments (368 653).
Larvae: are also marine, occurring over the inner continental shelf (149 322), but also occur in tidal passes and estuaries (1066).
Juveniles: prefer shallow estuarine areas including marsh creeks, tidal creeks and ditches, but they are also found in shallow bay areas and beaches, and occasionally offshore (363 543 591 725 853).
Adults: are abundant along sandy beaches and in bays and lagoons (791 846).  Predominantly an estuarine species commonly found in shallow estuaries throughout the Gulf of Mexico (327 653 692).

Substrate:  Black drum juveniles are said to prefer muddy bottoms in marsh habitats (543 591), but Edwards (1067) found that juveniles exhibited no preference for muddy bottoms over soft of hard packed sand bottoms in the Manatee River estuary, Florida.  Peters and McMichael (1069), working in Tampa Bay, collected juveniles in shallow, quiet, muddy-bottomed tidal creeks, rivers, secondary bays, and lagoons.  Adults usually found over sand and sandy beaches in coastal waters (791), but they also occur over sandy mud, mud, oyster bars, and worm reefs (139 543 692).

nodes.title: PHYSICAL/CHEMICAL
nodes.body:
Temperature:  Joseph, et al (368) proposed that eggs hatch in less than 24 hour at approximately 20.0 C.  In Tampa Bay, larvae were collected in temperatures ranging from 15.5 to 22.8 C (1069).  Eggs and larvae successfully develop at 18.0 to 20.0 C  (363 454) and have been collected in the wild at 11.0 - 21.0 C (149).  Adults tolerate a wide range of temperatures and have been collected in Texas at temperatures ranging between 3.0 and 35.0 C (653).  Sharp decreases in temperature cause movements to deeper waters (653).  Mass mortality is rather common along the Texas coast when water temperatures drop sharply and remain low for extended periods (653), but black drum were not among the species killed by numerous freezes at Sanibel Island, Florida (836 1068) or in the Indian River Lagoon (236).

Salinity:  Adults and juveniles are euryhaline found from 0.0 - 80.0 ppt (261 653); they are common at 9.0 - 26.0 ppt (454).  Laboratory spawned eggs hatched successfully at 8.8 to 34.0 ppt with highest survival occurring at 23 to 34 ppt (454).  Larvae were collected in Tampa bay when surface salinities ranged from 0.0 - 32.0 ppt (1069), and they have been collected elsewhere at 15 - 36 ppt (149).  Juveniles have been collected at salinities from 0.0 to 35.0 ppt in the Chesapeake and Delaware areas (363).  Juveniles have been collected in west Florida estuaries at the following salinities: 0.0 - 27.7 ppt at Charlotte Harbor (789), 16.6 - 32.3 ppt in Tampa Bay (664), and 20.6 - 26.1 ppt at Cedar Key (378).

nodes.title: REPRODUCTION
nodes.body:
Mode:  Sexes separate; fertilization by externally broadcast sexual products.

Mating and Spawning:  Males are soniferous and most spawning activity occurs one half hour before sunset for two to three hours (1058).  Black drum have been shown to spawn near passes and at the mouths of bays and lagoons (322 543 1069), but spawning also occurs within the Indian River Lagoon, open bays along the northern Gulf of Mexico and in the Chesapeake and Delaware areas (1058 368 653 725).  It has been suggested that spawning off the Texas coast occurs in waters ranging from 5 - 27 m deep (609).  In the Tampa Bay and Indian River Lagoon area, most spawning occurs in winter (beginning in November) or spring, with peak spawning in March and/or early April (1069 1058).  This period is similar to the spawning season reported elsewhere in the gulf by others (220 379 543 609 1070 1071).  Other Gulf studies report peak spawning in February and March (126 202 354 653). Evidence for limited spawning in December and January in Florida and Texas has also been reported (354 1069 1072).  Summer spawning has also been reported (543 1071 1073 1074).  Laboratory spawning has been achieved at 21 C and 28 - 31 ppt (230).

Reproductive Capacity:  One female 1110 mm long contained about 6,000,000 ova (543).  Average fecundity calculated after the examination of 451 females was 1,090,000 eggs (139).

nodes.title: GROWTH & DEVELOPMENT
nodes.body:
Eggs & larvae:  Eggs are 0.82_1.02 mm in diameter and contain 2 to 6 oil globules (368).  Eggs have been reported to hatch in 12-16 h and 24 h at 20o C (Alshuth and Gilmore 368).  Larvae are 1.9_2.7 mm TL at hatching (Alshuth and Gilmore 368).  Black drum larvae collected with plankton nets in Tampa Bay show an apparent modal increase in length from 2.5 mm on March 16 to 5.0 mm on March 29 for a growth rate of 0.2 mm/day (1069).  For black drum less than 50 mm, the equations best describing growth based on otolith data (1069) were:

[eq]
	L = _3.977 + 0.589A,   r^2 = 0.96  and,
	A = 2.412L _ 0.016(L_squared),   r_squared + 0.97
[/eq]
where:
	L = notochord length in mm and A = age in days

The Larvae collected in the Chesapeake and Delaware Bay region were reported to grow at about 0.2 mm/day at 21 C (368).

Juveniles:  Equations for size_at_age and age_at_size for 98 Tampa Bay black drum ranging from 2_160 mm were (1069):

[eq]
	L = _15.231 + 0.832A,  r_squared = 0.93   and,
	A = 11.772 + 1.624L _ 0.003(L_squared), r_squared = 0.94
[/eq]
where: L = standard length in mm and A = age in days

Overall growth rate from hatching to 150 mm would average 0.8 mm/day, and growth from 35 - 150 mm would average 0.9 mm/day (1069).  In upper Tampa Bay, Price and Schlueter (853) reported an increase in length from 26.7 mm SL in May to 92.0 mm SL in August.  Black drum reach 140 - 180 mm SL at the end of the first year; 210 - 250 mm SL at 1.5 years; and 290 - 330 mm SL in two years (653).  Texas studies indicate females reach maturity at 275 - 320 mm TL when at the end of their second year (543 653).  Studies conducted in northeast Florida found mature males at sizes beginning at 450 - 499 mm TL at age 2 (497).  Northeast Florida females matured when older and slightly longer with maturation occurring between 650 - 699 mm TL at age 5 or 6 (497).

Adults:  Simmons and Breuer (653) reported adults growing to 400 - 430 mm SL by the end of the third year; beyond that tag returns indicated a growth of 50 mm/year.  Murphy and Taylor (497) reported growth rates of black drum from northeast Florida at about 100 mm/year for age 1- 3 fish, slowing to 10 - 30 mm/year for ages 15-20.  Growth rates for black drum from Virginia, Georgia, northeast Florida, and Texas are presented by Murphy and Taylor (497).  Growth rates were similar in all areas with the exception of older fish being smaller in Georgia and Texas (497).  Equations for weight-length and length-length relationships for northeast Florida black drum are also presented by Murphy and Taylor (497).  Based on size, some black drum may live as long as 35 years (47), while otolith studies in Florida indicate they may live as long as 58 years (497).  Adults occasionally attain weights over 45.3 kg (100 lbs), and the largest black drum caught has been variously reported as 50 kg (109 lbs)(788), 52.2 kg (113 lbs)(1075), and 66.3 kg (146 lbs)(102).  Smith (834) reported one specimen from Florida as weighing 66.2 kg 9146 lbs), and this could be the same fish later reported by Cave (102).  Smith (834) also stated that drum weighing 18 - 27 kg (40 - 60 lbs) were common in North Carolina early in the 1900`s.

nodes.title: FOOD & FEEDING
nodes.body:
Miles (467) found that drum in Aransas Bay, Texas fed heavily on shrimp, mollusks, and aquatic vegetation but only slightly on fish.  Some plant material has also been found that was probably ingested incidentally, and all fish examined from several Texas estuaries had been feeding on dead shell with Acetabularia and other algae attached (653).  The consumption of soft food decreases as size increases with adult drum shifting to mollusks and crabs (189 543 1069).  Martin (439) reported that black drum > 300 mm TL favored bivalve mollusks, with Mulinia lateralis most frequently encountered.  Dugas (189) found black drum >700 mm SL prey on oysters about 75 mm in length.  Another study observed that drum <900 mm TL consumed oysters 25 - 75 mm in length while drum >900 mm TL consumed oysters 25 - 115 in length (102).

Larvae: feed primarily on zooplankton (47).

Juveniles: Small juveniles feed on an assortment of items including amphipods, small fish, polychaetes, and crustaceans including copepods (439 543 653 725 1069).  One study found that small juveniles consumed pelecypod siphon tips (1069).

Adults: The major food organism groups of adult drum, in order of importance, are arthropods (mostly crustaceans), mollusks (mostly bivalves), annelids, and fish (189). Other prey items include: Rangia cuneata, Mercenaria mercenaria, Ensis minor, tellin clams, xanthid crabs, insects, mysids, amphipods, barnacles, isopods, penaeid shrimp, mud shrimp, hermit crabs, Callinectes sapidus, polychaetes, Anchoa mitchilli, Chaetodipterus faber, gobies, and Micropogonias undulatus (102 189).

nodes.title: ECOLOGICAL INTERACTIONS & NOTES
nodes.body:
A marine cestode (the pleurocercoid stage), commonly called the ?spaghetti worm? infects the flesh causing it to have low or no value to the fisherman.  The cestode poses no health threat by human consumption (653).  Other authors also reported the presence of parasitic worm, and stated that fishermen refer to drum as a ?wormy? fish (312 834).

The long life span of black drum implies an extremely low natural mortality rate which probably means that little surplus production is available for commercial fishery yield (497).  This species appears to be a poor candidate for an intensive or even moderate fishery because populations could be depleted by growth overfishing (497).

The normal feeding habits of black drum may have a detrimental effect on the spawning and nursery grounds of spotted seatrout, Cynoscion nebulosus, red drum, Sciaenops ocellatus, and juvenile penaeid shrimp by the destruction of seagrass beds (102).

sections.heading: Movements/Migrations
sections.content: Black drum are predominantly estuarine inhabitants, and little inter-bay movement has been recorded in Texas waters (653).  Richards (591) considered the species to be migratory along the mid-Atlantic coast, exhibiting a northerly and inshore movement in the spring, and a movement to the south and offshore in late fall.  A similar but less well defined migration may occur in the Laguna Madre area of Texas (653).  Adults display spawning migrations toward Gulf passes in Texas (653), and toward the mouth of the bay in the Chesapeake area (591).  Following spawning, adults disperse back into the estuarine environment at both locations (591 653).  Adverse conditions such as high temperatures, hypersalinity or insufficient food may trigger localized migrations to areas with more favorable conditions (653).

sections.heading: LIFE MODE
sections.content:
Eggs: are pelagic (368).
Larvae: are also pelagic, and are transported by currents through tidal passes to estuarine waters (9 368).
Juveniles: prefer shallow, turbid, nutrient rich waters (543), and are commonly found in estuaries (791).
Adults: are pelagic throughout the estuaries and bays of the Gulf (139 653), and are often abundant along beaches (791).  At maturity, adults are in constant movement searching for food, which often results in the formation of large schools (591).

sections.heading: Type
sections.content:
Eggs: are found in both marine and estuarine environments (368 653).
Larvae: are also marine, occurring over the inner continental shelf (149 322), but also occur in tidal passes and estuaries (1066).
Juveniles: prefer shallow estuarine areas including marsh creeks, tidal creeks and ditches, but they are also found in shallow bay areas and beaches, and occasionally offshore (363 543 591 725 853).
Adults: are abundant along sandy beaches and in bays and lagoons (791 846).  Predominantly an estuarine species commonly found in shallow estuaries throughout the Gulf of Mexico (327 653 692).

Substrate:  Black drum juveniles are said to prefer muddy bottoms in marsh habitats (543 591), but Edwards (1067) found that juveniles exhibited no preference for muddy bottoms over soft of hard packed sand bottoms in the Manatee River estuary, Florida.  Peters and McMichael (1069), working in Tampa Bay, collected juveniles in shallow, quiet, muddy-bottomed tidal creeks, rivers, secondary bays, and lagoons.  Adults usually found over sand and sandy beaches in coastal waters (791), but they also occur over sandy mud, mud, oyster bars, and worm reefs (139 543 692).

sections.heading: PHYSICAL/CHEMICAL
sections.content:
Temperature:  Joseph, et al (368) proposed that eggs hatch in less than 24 hour at approximately 20.0 C.  In Tampa Bay, larvae were collected in temperatures ranging from 15.5 to 22.8 C (1069).  Eggs and larvae successfully develop at 18.0 to 20.0 C  (363 454) and have been collected in the wild at 11.0 - 21.0 C (149).  Adults tolerate a wide range of temperatures and have been collected in Texas at temperatures ranging between 3.0 and 35.0 C (653).  Sharp decreases in temperature cause movements to deeper waters (653).  Mass mortality is rather common along the Texas coast when water temperatures drop sharply and remain low for extended periods (653), but black drum were not among the species killed by numerous freezes at Sanibel Island, Florida (836 1068) or in the Indian River Lagoon (236).

Salinity:  Adults and juveniles are euryhaline found from 0.0 - 80.0 ppt (261 653); they are common at 9.0 - 26.0 ppt (454).  Laboratory spawned eggs hatched successfully at 8.8 to 34.0 ppt with highest survival occurring at 23 to 34 ppt (454).  Larvae were collected in Tampa bay when surface salinities ranged from 0.0 - 32.0 ppt (1069), and they have been collected elsewhere at 15 - 36 ppt (149).  Juveniles have been collected at salinities from 0.0 to 35.0 ppt in the Chesapeake and Delaware areas (363).  Juveniles have been collected in west Florida estuaries at the following salinities: 0.0 - 27.7 ppt at Charlotte Harbor (789), 16.6 - 32.3 ppt in Tampa Bay (664), and 20.6 - 26.1 ppt at Cedar Key (378).

sections.heading: REPRODUCTION
sections.content:
Mode:  Sexes separate; fertilization by externally broadcast sexual products.

Mating and Spawning:  Males are soniferous and most spawning activity occurs one half hour before sunset for two to three hours (1058).  Black drum have been shown to spawn near passes and at the mouths of bays and lagoons (322 543 1069), but spawning also occurs within the Indian River Lagoon, open bays along the northern Gulf of Mexico and in the Chesapeake and Delaware areas (1058 368 653 725).  It has been suggested that spawning off the Texas coast occurs in waters ranging from 5 - 27 m deep (609).  In the Tampa Bay and Indian River Lagoon area, most spawning occurs in winter (beginning in November) or spring, with peak spawning in March and/or early April (1069 1058).  This period is similar to the spawning season reported elsewhere in the gulf by others (220 379 543 609 1070 1071).  Other Gulf studies report peak spawning in February and March (126 202 354 653). Evidence for limited spawning in December and January in Florida and Texas has also been reported (354 1069 1072).  Summer spawning has also been reported (543 1071 1073 1074).  Laboratory spawning has been achieved at 21 C and 28 - 31 ppt (230).

Reproductive Capacity:  One female 1110 mm long contained about 6,000,000 ova (543).  Average fecundity calculated after the examination of 451 females was 1,090,000 eggs (139).

sections.heading: GROWTH & DEVELOPMENT
sections.content:
Eggs & larvae:  Eggs are 0.82_1.02 mm in diameter and contain 2 to 6 oil globules (368).  Eggs have been reported to hatch in 12-16 h and 24 h at 20o C (Alshuth and Gilmore 368).  Larvae are 1.9_2.7 mm TL at hatching (Alshuth and Gilmore 368).  Black drum larvae collected with plankton nets in Tampa Bay show an apparent modal increase in length from 2.5 mm on March 16 to 5.0 mm on March 29 for a growth rate of 0.2 mm/day (1069).  For black drum less than 50 mm, the equations best describing growth based on otolith data (1069) were:

[eq]
	L = _3.977 + 0.589A,   r^2 = 0.96  and,
	A = 2.412L _ 0.016(L_squared),   r_squared + 0.97
[/eq]
where:
	L = notochord length in mm and A = age in days

The Larvae collected in the Chesapeake and Delaware Bay region were reported to grow at about 0.2 mm/day at 21 C (368).

Juveniles:  Equations for size_at_age and age_at_size for 98 Tampa Bay black drum ranging from 2_160 mm were (1069):

[eq]
	L = _15.231 + 0.832A,  r_squared = 0.93   and,
	A = 11.772 + 1.624L _ 0.003(L_squared), r_squared = 0.94
[/eq]
where: L = standard length in mm and A = age in days

Overall growth rate from hatching to 150 mm would average 0.8 mm/day, and growth from 35 - 150 mm would average 0.9 mm/day (1069).  In upper Tampa Bay, Price and Schlueter (853) reported an increase in length from 26.7 mm SL in May to 92.0 mm SL in August.  Black drum reach 140 - 180 mm SL at the end of the first year; 210 - 250 mm SL at 1.5 years; and 290 - 330 mm SL in two years (653).  Texas studies indicate females reach maturity at 275 - 320 mm TL when at the end of their second year (543 653).  Studies conducted in northeast Florida found mature males at sizes beginning at 450 - 499 mm TL at age 2 (497).  Northeast Florida females matured when older and slightly longer with maturation occurring between 650 - 699 mm TL at age 5 or 6 (497).

Adults:  Simmons and Breuer (653) reported adults growing to 400 - 430 mm SL by the end of the third year; beyond that tag returns indicated a growth of 50 mm/year.  Murphy and Taylor (497) reported growth rates of black drum from northeast Florida at about 100 mm/year for age 1- 3 fish, slowing to 10 - 30 mm/year for ages 15-20.  Growth rates for black drum from Virginia, Georgia, northeast Florida, and Texas are presented by Murphy and Taylor (497).  Growth rates were similar in all areas with the exception of older fish being smaller in Georgia and Texas (497).  Equations for weight-length and length-length relationships for northeast Florida black drum are also presented by Murphy and Taylor (497).  Based on size, some black drum may live as long as 35 years (47), while otolith studies in Florida indicate they may live as long as 58 years (497).  Adults occasionally attain weights over 45.3 kg (100 lbs), and the largest black drum caught has been variously reported as 50 kg (109 lbs)(788), 52.2 kg (113 lbs)(1075), and 66.3 kg (146 lbs)(102).  Smith (834) reported one specimen from Florida as weighing 66.2 kg 9146 lbs), and this could be the same fish later reported by Cave (102).  Smith (834) also stated that drum weighing 18 - 27 kg (40 - 60 lbs) were common in North Carolina early in the 1900`s.

sections.heading: FOOD & FEEDING
sections.content:
Miles (467) found that drum in Aransas Bay, Texas fed heavily on shrimp, mollusks, and aquatic vegetation but only slightly on fish.  Some plant material has also been found that was probably ingested incidentally, and all fish examined from several Texas estuaries had been feeding on dead shell with Acetabularia and other algae attached (653).  The consumption of soft food decreases as size increases with adult drum shifting to mollusks and crabs (189 543 1069).  Martin (439) reported that black drum > 300 mm TL favored bivalve mollusks, with Mulinia lateralis most frequently encountered.  Dugas (189) found black drum >700 mm SL prey on oysters about 75 mm in length.  Another study observed that drum <900 mm TL consumed oysters 25 - 75 mm in length while drum >900 mm TL consumed oysters 25 - 115 in length (102).

Larvae: feed primarily on zooplankton (47).

Juveniles: Small juveniles feed on an assortment of items including amphipods, small fish, polychaetes, and crustaceans including copepods (439 543 653 725 1069).  One study found that small juveniles consumed pelecypod siphon tips (1069).

Adults: The major food organism groups of adult drum, in order of importance, are arthropods (mostly crustaceans), mollusks (mostly bivalves), annelids, and fish (189). Other prey items include: Rangia cuneata, Mercenaria mercenaria, Ensis minor, tellin clams, xanthid crabs, insects, mysids, amphipods, barnacles, isopods, penaeid shrimp, mud shrimp, hermit crabs, Callinectes sapidus, polychaetes, Anchoa mitchilli, Chaetodipterus faber, gobies, and Micropogonias undulatus (102 189).

sections.heading: ECOLOGICAL INTERACTIONS & NOTES
sections.content:
A marine cestode (the pleurocercoid stage), commonly called the ?spaghetti worm? infects the flesh causing it to have low or no value to the fisherman.  The cestode poses no health threat by human consumption (653).  Other authors also reported the presence of parasitic worm, and stated that fishermen refer to drum as a ?wormy? fish (312 834).

The long life span of black drum implies an extremely low natural mortality rate which probably means that little surplus production is available for commercial fishery yield (497).  This species appears to be a poor candidate for an intensive or even moderate fishery because populations could be depleted by growth overfishing (497).

The normal feeding habits of black drum may have a detrimental effect on the spawning and nursery grounds of spotted seatrout, Cynoscion nebulosus, red drum, Sciaenops ocellatus, and juvenile penaeid shrimp by the destruction of seagrass beds (102).
